book.Title: {{W|The Thunder Book}}
book.page:
[[The First Crack]]
Before the first word there was a silence, and the silence was not empty. It was wound tight, the way a tendon is wound, the way a held breath is wound.
Then something let go.
The old people of the salt did not say that thunder *spoke*. They said it *remembered* -- that every crack was an answer to a question asked so long ago that the asking had worn away and only the answer was left, rolling.

[[On the Charge]]
A body holds a certain quantity of stillness. Call it what you like. The salt-diggers called it the dry account, and they kept it carefully, because a person who spends all their stillness at once does not get it back the way they lost it.
But there is another account, kept in a different ledger, and it is not spent downward. It is spent *outward*. Press it into a stone and the stone grows warm. Press it into a wound and the wound forgets to close.
The trick is not to hold more. The trick is to hold it *differently*.

[[On the Fan and the Coil]]
Current, once released, forgets where it was going. It finds the nearest path down and takes it, and then the next, and the next, until the ground has drunk it. This is why the untutored call lightning and are answered by a scorch on their own boots.
To shape it you must first teach it a direction, and the direction must be wider than a finger and narrower than an arm. The old diagrams show it as a fan of reeds.
Where the reeds are widest, the current is thinnest. Where they are gathered, it bites.

[[On the Ledger of Storms]]
Every storm keeps a ledger, and the entries are not written in ink.
This copy is one leaf of that ledger, torn out and pressed flat, and the rest of the leaves are scattered where the ground remembers the sea.
The salt keeps one. The stone keeps one. The broken places keep one, and the wet places keep one, and none of them will simply hand it over.
Read what you can from this page. It will tell you where to look, if you ask it properly.

[[A Caution]]
Do not read this book in the rain.
* -- the hand that copied this leaf, unsigned*
